                                      I.     SUMMARY

       This Initial Paper Hearing Brief and Dr. Lesser’s Affidavit (Exh. NEC-005)

generally follow the analytical process outlined by the Commission in Coakley v.

Bangor Hydro-Electric Co., Opinion No. 594, 194 FERC ¶ 61,208 (2026) (“Opinion No.

594”). This Brief and Dr. Lesser’s Affidavit first discuss and explain where the

NECOS agree and disagree with the analyses presented by the New England

Transmission Owners (“NETOs”) for their proposed snapback of their return on

common equity (“ROE”) to 11.39 percent, 25 basis points above pre-Opinion No. 531

levels. As the FPA Section 205 proponents of a 182 basis point increase over the 9.57

percent “base” return on common equity (“ROE”) found just and reasonable in

Opinion No. 594, the NETOs bear the burden of proof in this proceeding 4 and have

failed to satisfy it.

 A.    Proxy Group Construction

      Dr. Lesser constructs a DCF proxy group beginning with the 37 companies

listed by Value Line as “electric utilities,” which his analysis winnows to a DCF proxy

group of 25. NETOs’ witness Mr. McKenzie begins with the same 37 companies, and

then adds Algonquin Power & Utilities Corporation, which is neither a Value Line

electric utility nor even followed by Value Line. Dr. Lesser excludes Algonquin from

his DCF proxy group because, as he explains, Algonquin does not actually meet the

Commission’s alternative criterion for including companies that are not Value Line

electric utilities in an electric utility proxy group: “the preponderance of a company's

business activities is in the sale of electricity.” 5 Dr. Lesser and Mr. McKenzie both

exclude from their respective DCF proxy groups: (1) Hawaiian Electric Company and

Pacific Gas & Electric Company because they lack investment grade credit ratings,

(2) Black Hills Energy, NorthWestern Corporation and TXNM Energy due to merger

and acquisition activity during the study period, and (3) Edison International due to

uncertainty sufficient to distort DCF inputs surrounding its financial exposure in

connection with the Eaton Fire. Both Dr. Lesser and Mr. McKenzie omit Otter Tail

Corporation and Hydro One, Inc. from their DCF analysis because neither had a

published I/B/E/S earnings growth rate as of March 31, 2026.

      Dr. Lesser included two utilities in his proxy group that NETOs’ witness Mr.

McKenzie had excluded from his DCF proxy group: Fortis, Inc. (which owns Tucson

more accurate results than the use of Value Line betas. 17

                                      II.     ARGUMENT

      The “primary aim of [the FPA] is the protection of consumers from excessive

rates and charges.” 29 In determining a just and reasonable rate of return, defined as

“the cost to the utility of raising capital,” 30 the Commission must balance the interests

of a utility’s investors against the “public interest against excessive rates.” 31 Hope

and Bluefield establish that this balance is reached by an ROE that is no higher than

what is required to: (1) maintain the financial integrity of the utility whose ROE is

being determined; (2) permit it to raise capital sufficient to discharge its mission; and

(3) achieve a return commensurate with the returns earned by comparable risk

enterprises. 32 A just and reasonable ROE must also reflect current market conditions

      The Commission has long held that its obligations under the Federal Power

Act and Hope and Bluefield require it to set a regulated return that reflects the

market cost of equity capital. 34 In Order No. 461 the Commission found “compelling

economic justification for relying on the market cost of capital as the standard for

an ROE that reflects the market cost of equity capital:

         [T]he cost of capital of a regulated firm represents precisely the
         expected return that investors could anticipate from other
         investments while bearing no more and no less risk, and since
         investors will not provide capital unless the investment is
         expected to yield its opportunity cost of capital, the
         correspondence of the definition of the cost of capital with the
         court’s definition of legally required earnings appears clear. Hope
         refers to both: commensurate earnings and the attraction of
         capital. These two approaches are harmonized when the allowed
         rate of return is set equal to the cost of capital. 36

Algonquin was ultimately excluded from the NETOs’ DCF and CAPM analyses based

B.    There Is No Longer Any Factual Basis for 80 Percent Weighting of

        C.       Calculation of MRP for the CAPM Methodology

22.     As discussed in more detail in Section III.C, below, and as I explained in a recent article
        published in the Energy Law Journal, 8 the Commission’s MRP estimation methodology is
        inconsistent with both the tenets of the CAPM itself and with basic economic logic. The
        Commission’s methodology for inferring the market risk premium component of the
        CAPM analysis erroneously conflates the S&P 500, which is a market proxy, with all
        marketable assets, which is the basis of the CAPM. Consequently, the Commission’s MRP
        methodology assumes that the returns to the entire market can grow rapidly forever. The
        result is that the forecast total earnings of the S&P 500 firms quickly exceed the historical
        relationship between total corporate earnings and U.S. gross domestic product (“GDP”),
        and exceed the entire U.S. GDP within the Commission’s assumed 50-year timeline. 9 The
        former is inconsistent with observed historical data over the last 75 years; the latter is
        mathematically impossible by definition, because corporate income is one component of
        total GDP.

23.     Moreover, the Commission’s MRP methodology produces estimates that are at odds with
        those of major financial institutions and academics. Although the Commission has
        previously cited academic literature dating back to the 1980s and 1990s to support its MRP
        methodology, the flaws in that literature were later corrected in subsequent academic
        publications. These later publications exposed the logical flaws in the literature on which
        the Commission’s current MRP calculation methodology relies by recognizing the
        impossibility of indefinite, rapid growth in corporate earnings far above competitive
        industry norms (called “excessive” or “anomalous” earnings) and by developing a revised
        estimation framework to account for those excessive earnings. That framework yields MRP
        values that are consistent with economic logic. (Furthermore, indefinite and rapid growth
        in corporate earnings inevitably would lead to antitrust issues.)

24.     Although the Commission has previously addressed certain challenges to its MRP
        methodology, it has not yet addressed the issues outlined in this affidavit concerning the
        inconsistency of the results produced by that methodology with historical empirical
        observations, contemporaneous market opinion, current economic analysis, and
        mathematical logic.

85.   The Commission should reject the request by the PTOs to set the base ROE to 11.39% and

      adjustments to the Commission’s Opinion No. 594 methodology proposed in this affidavit:

      weighting in the Commission’s Opinion No. 594 DCF analysis, (2) applying a two-thirds
      short-term, one-third long-term, weighted average growth rate in calculating the market
      risk premium component of the CAPM analysis, and (3) relying on the median of the range
      of reasonableness, rather than the midpoint, to set the just and reasonable return on equity.
      In the alternative, if the Commission rejects my revised DCF analysis, but accepts the
      alternative CAPM analysis, then it should set the base allowed ROE to 9.33%, or if it
      continues to rely on the average of the midpoint values, 9.46%.

      DCF methodology, but rejects my alternative MRP calculation, then I recommend the

making. 3

                                   I. INTRODUCTION
      Determining a just and reasonable allowed return on equity for regulated
companies is a crucial aspect of the cost-based regulation approach employed by
FERC and most state utility regulators. 8 As enunciated in Hope, to ensure
regulated companies have sufficient access to capital to maintain reliable service,
they must provide investors with an expected return that reflects prevailing market
conditions at the time. However, because such a just and reasonable return on
equity is not observable, it must be estimated, and various methodologies have
been developed to do so. Some of these, including the DCF and CAPM, are
market-based, that is, they account for current conditions in financial markets.
Others, such as the Comparable Earnings approach, are not. 9
      The allowed ROE is a component of a regulated firm’s overall cost of capital,
which includes all sources of investment funds, principally equity and debt.
Ascertaining the expected return on equity investors require, given current market
conditions, which is defined as the market cost of equity capital, 10 “is a standard
of finance resting on stubborn facts.” 11 Any reasoned analysis of the market cost
of equity capital rests on the efficient market hypothesis (EMH), which is “[t]he
cornerstone of modern investment theory.” 12 As the Court stated in Tennessee,
“[i]n its ‘semi-strong’ form, the hypothesis says that stock prices will react
promptly to new public releases of information.” 13 Thus, under the EMH, the price
of a stock today is based on investors’ collective expectations of the present value
of the stock’s future cash flows. Moreover, the EMH means that only a return that
reflects current market conditions can satisfy the comparative risk requirements of
Hope and Bluefield, 14 and the Commission’s “mandate to ensure that rates are

                     IV. FERC’S IMPLEMENTATION OF THE CAPM
      The CAPM evolved from the theory of portfolio risk and the insight that the
risk of holding a portfolio of many assets ultimately reflects only their relative risk

investors can maximize their return for a given level of risk by holding a mix of
the “market” portfolio made up of all financial assets, and a risk-free asset, usually
assumed to be a U.S. government Treasury bond.

methodology results. 72 Subsequently, in 2018, it proposed fully incorporating the
CAPM methodology to determine an overall range of reasonableness by averaging
the low values and high values of the different methodologies. 73 FERC formally
accepted the equal weighting of CAPM results with DCF results in Opinion
No.569. 74

forecast. For example, the same Staff testimony noted above used a long-term
GDP forecast of 4.08%. 97 Using the 12.41% expected market return and the

methodology, the resulting expected market return would be (2/3) × (12.17%) +
(1/3) × (4.08%) = 9.47%. Subtracting the 4.66% average yield on 30-year U.S.
Treasury bonds results in an MRP of 4.81%. That is far closer to financial firms’
estimates of the MRP, such as those prepared by Kroll, which the Commission
relies on for size premium data. 98

                     V. FERC’S RISK PREMIUM METHODOLOGY
      The RP methodology shares similarities with the CAPM. However, unlike
the CAPM, the RP methodology is based on the historically observed premium
between equity returns and bond yields. In Opinion No. 531, the Commission
accepted a version of the RP methodology used by the NETOs, which was based
on a simple linear regression model of previously authorized ROE values versus
utility bond yields (Figure 4). 99 Specifically, the model estimated was:

                                  RP j ,t = a + b × Yb ,t + ε e ,t , (10)

where RPj,t = (ROEj,t – Yb,t ) is the risk premium associated with previous FERC
decision j, Yb,t is the average yield on long-term utility bonds at the time of each
decision, a and b are constants to be estimated, and εe,t is an error term. In some
cases, the historical data is based on annual averages, while in others it may be
based on the allowed ROE at the time of each FERC decision.

between 2006 and 2016. 100 As shown, the resulting regression is RP = 0.0872 –
0.6806×Y. FERC uses the estimated equation (which changes depending on the
data used to estimate it) to calculate a risk premium based on the average Baa-
bond yield over the particular study period. For example, if the average bond yield
was 5.0%, then RP = 0.0782 – 0.6806 × 0.05 = 4.42%. Hence, the corresponding
allowed ROE would equal 5.0% + 4.42% = 9.42%.

methodology from the long-rejected CE methodology. As described by Roger
Morin, the CE methodology examines the book returns of a proxy group of
unregulated companies deemed to have comparable risk to the company under
review, 122 the rationale being that the company under review should earn a similar
book return as these unregulated companies. Importantly, unregulated companies
are selected to avoid a circularity problem arising by selecting a group of FERC-
regulated companies and evaluating their book returns, which are affected by
previous FERC decisions, to establish a return for a FERC-regulated company.
Yet, FERC’s EE methodology was based on the same proxy group of utilities used
for the DCF and CAPM analyses. As with the RP methodology, the EE
methodology is inherently circular because book returns of regulated companies
will be determined, in part, by FERC’s setting of allowed ROEs.
     Another fundamental problem with using book returns is that those returns
will differ depending on how companies account for their costs. Although U.S.
companies follow Generally Accepted Accounting Practices (GAAP), 123 those
practices do not ensure absolute uniformity in how different companies treat
certain costs. For example, different companies will depreciate capital
investments at different rates. Book returns also depend on capital structure, the
timing of capital investments, and how those investments are financed.

requirements of Hope and Bluefield. The EE methodology is not based on
prevailing market conditions and thus provides no information on comparable risk.
